<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Beichen Wan
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Mo Liu
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Paul Grigas
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Zuo-Jun Max Shen
</span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider the sequential experimental design problem in the predict-then-optimize paradigm. In this paradigm, the outputs of the prediction model are used as coefficient vectors in a downstream linear optimization problem. Traditional sequential experimental design aims to control the input variables (features) so that the improvement in prediction accuracy from each experimental outcome (label) is maximized. However, in the predict-then-optimize setting, performance is ultimately evaluated based on the decision loss induced by the downstream optimization, rather than by prediction error. This mismatch between prediction accuracy and decision loss renders traditional decision-blind designs inefficient.
<span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Methodology/results:</span> To address this issue, we propose a directional-based metric to quantify predictive uncertainty. This metric does not require solving an optimization oracle and is therefore computationally tractable. We show that the resulting sequential design criterion enjoys strong consistency and convergence guarantees.
<span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Managerial implications:</span> Under a broad class of distributions, we demonstrate that our directional uncertainty–based design attains an earlier stopping time than decision-blind designs. This advantage is further supported by real-world experiments on an LLM job allocation problem.</p>

<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Experimental design studies how to strategically collect data by choosing experiments to run (i.e., which features to collect labels for) in order to maximize the information gained from experimental outcomes. It has long served as a fundamental tool for data collection. By carefully designing informative experiments, one can collect labeled data that supports the construction of predictive models. Here, the labeled data refers to pairs of (group, response) or, equivalently, (feature, label) or (covariate, outcome). Under a limited labeling budget, the goal of experimental design is to identify data acquisition strategies that lead to an accurate and reliable prediction model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This data collection problem becomes particularly important when labels are expensive or time-consuming to obtain, especially in sequential settings where experiments are conducted over time and each newly observed label informs which experiment to run next. For example, in AI training, human annotators may be required to evaluate prompts for large language models (LLMs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al. 2022</a>)</cite>, whereas in clinical trials, recruiting participants and measuring outcomes involve ethical, temporal, and financial constraints <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anderer et al. 2022</a>)</cite>. Classical experimental design provides a rich framework for controlling inputs (e.g., covariates or feature configurations) to maximize the information gained from corresponding outputs (e.g., treatment responses or outcomes).
Because the information gained from labeling depends on the labeled data already collected, sequential experimental design chooses the next experiment adaptively based on past observations to maximize expected information gain (or uncertainty reduction) about the target of interest <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Castro et al. 2005</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sugiyama and Nakajima 2009</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cai et al. 2016</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Beygelzimer et al. 2009</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In sequential experimental design, the “value” of a candidate label depends on how uncertainty and performance are measured. Much of the regression-oriented literature optimizes surrogate objectives tied to (squared) prediction error, implicitly assuming that uniformly reducing predictive uncertainty translates into improved task performance. However, in many scenarios, the output of a predictive model is used directly as input to a downstream optimization problem to determine a decision policy (e.g., setting prices or choosing order quantities). In this setting, often referred to as the predict-then-optimize and/or contextual optimization setting, the performance metric of primary interest is the <em id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">decision loss</em> induced by decisions made using the model’s predictions, rather than a standalone measure of predictive error. Consequently, smaller predictive uncertainty does not always imply smaller decision loss, as illustrated in Section <a href="#S1.SS2" title="1.2 Application Example: Contextual Job Assignment ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1.2</span></a>. This observation motivates the study of sequential experimental design with a decision-focused approach.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we focus on the predict-then-optimize setting where the downstream decision problem is a linear optimization problem. Designing optimal sequential policies in this setting is challenging because uncertainty propagates through multiple stages: predictive uncertainty perturbs the parameters of the downstream optimization problem, and these perturbations translate discontinuously into changes in decisions (e.g., order quantities in inventory management or allocation choices in transportation systems). These decision changes further propagate into changes in decision loss. Consequently, relying on simple prediction-uncertainty proxies is misleading and inefficient for evaluating uncertainty in final decisions. On the other hand, directly evaluating uncertainty in decision loss is often both computationally and statistically intractable.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">To design a sequential data collection metric that is both aligned with decision loss and computationally tractable, we propose a <em id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">directional uncertainty</em>-guided approach. Building on the theoretical observation that the scale of the prediction does not affect decision-making in linear optimization (Fact <a href="#Thmthm1" title="Fact 1 (Fact 1: The SPO loss is scale invariant.) ‣ 2.1 Algorithm Motivation ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), our design method concentrates on the <em id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">directional</em> information of predictions. The central idea is to normalize each predicted cost vector onto the unit ball before evaluating its associated uncertainty. This normalization emphasizes how prediction errors project onto decision-relevant directions that influence the resulting downstream actions.
Through this lens, our approach yields data acquisition rules that prioritize designs that are informative for downstream decisions, while de-emphasizing uncertainties that are irrelevant to decision making.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Since this directional-guided design method does not require solving the downstream optimization problem, it is straightforward to implement and intuitively appealing. However, an important question remains:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Can the simple normalization of predictions yield a data collection metric that is better aligned with decision making and provides stronger theoretical guarantees?</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we answer this question by showing that the directional uncertainty–based design approach achieves a strictly earlier stopping time than decision-blind designs that rely solely on prediction uncertainty. Our key contributions are summarized as follows.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For contextual stochastic linear optimization, we introduce a decision-focused sequential experimental design method that prioritizes labels according to <em id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">directional uncertainty</em>. This design method is motivated by the fact that the downstream linear optimization is independent of the prediction scale.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We establish non-asymptotic guarantees for our directional uncertainty-guided design method in terms of the excess decision-risk bounds. By comparing the stopping time, we show that in general, our directional uncertainty-based method is no worse than traditional prediction uncertainty-based design methods.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Under a mild <em id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">suboptimality gap</em> assumption, which states that there exists a positive gap in expected decision loss between optimal prediction models and suboptimal ones (Assumption <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Comparison Under Optimality Gap Assumption ‣ 3 Comparison with Decision-blind Sequential Design ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>), we prove that our method achieves an earlier stopping time than decision-blind benchmark algorithms. This result highlights the benefit of normalization in experimental design in the predict-then-optimize setting. We further provide natural examples of distributions that satisfy the suboptimality gap assumption in Section <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Examples of Optimality Gap ‣ 4 Justifications and Examples of Assumptions ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Through numerical experiments based on a dataset for cardiovascular disease diagnosis as well as a <em id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">real-world</em> study on prompt engineering for LLMs, we show that our policy attains the same decision risk with substantially less data than supervised or decision-blind sequential alternatives. These results confirm the practical advantages of the directional uncertainty-based approach.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S1.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p10.1" class="ltx_p">The organization of the main body is as follows. In Section <a href="#S1.SS1" title="1.1 Sequential Design for Predict-then-Optimize ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1.1</span></a>, we introduce the formulation and setting of sequential experimental design in the predict-then-optimize setting. To illustrate the practical importance of this problem, we present a motivating application in Section  <a href="#S1.SS2" title="1.2 Application Example: Contextual Job Assignment ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1.2</span></a>. Section <a href="#S1.SS3" title="1.3 Related Work ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1.3</span></a> reviews related work on decision-focused learning and experimental design. Our algorithm and its theoretical guarantees are provided in Section <a href="#S2" title="2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. To further highlight the advantage of the directional-uncertainty approach, Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Comparison with Decision-blind Sequential Design ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> considers a class of distributions under which the proposed method guarantees an earlier stopping time than the decision-blind benchmark. Justifications of the assumptions are given in Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Justifications and Examples of Assumptions ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Numerical Study ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> examines the numerical performance of our sequential design method in two contexts—cardiovascular diagnosis and LLM job assignment. Both studies demonstrate that the directional–uncertainty–based design can achieve an earlier stopping time than traditional benchmarks. Finally, the conclusion is provided in Section <a href="#S6" title="6 Conclusion ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">1.1 </span>Sequential Design for Predict-then-Optimize</h3>

<div id="S1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we introduce the sequential experimental design problem in the <span id="S1.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">predict-then-optimize</span> paradigm, which is a popular class of methods for addressing contextual stochastic linear optimization. In this setting, a decision maker (also a data collector) uses the collected data to fit a predictive model that predicts the unknown parameters in the downstream decision-making problem. Specifically, the decision-making problem is a linear optimization problem with unknown coefficients in the objective function. (For example, a logistics planner needs to select shipping routes for future deliveries, but must first predict fuel costs or travel times based on observable contextual features such as weather or traffic conditions.) The sequential design focuses on the data collection stage, where, by actively designing experiments, the (noisy) outcome of the designed experiments can be observed. The ultimate goal is to use a small number of experiments to obtain a prediction model that minimizes the expected decision loss.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Let us first specify some notation used throughout the paper. We use <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\|\cdot\|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0em">∥</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\cdot\|</annotation></semantics></math> to denote the <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> norm. Let the sample space <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathcal{X}}=\{\mathrm{X}_{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathcal{X}}=\{\mathrm{X}_{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{m}</annotation></semantics></math> be the set of possible designs (treatments), where each <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{X}_{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{\kappa}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>κ</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{X}_{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{\kappa}</annotation></semantics></math> stands for a possible design vector. Let <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mo>⊆</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the space of possible outcomes (i.e., the label space). We use <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math> to denote the unknown joint distribution of the design <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and the outcome <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>. Since we focus on predicting the relationship between the feature <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\in\mathcal{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\in\mathcal{X}</annotation></semantics></math> and the outcome <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c\in\mathcal{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c\in\mathcal{C}</annotation></semantics></math>, for simplicity, we assume for any <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=\mathrm{X}_{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=\mathrm{X}_{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math>, the marginal density of <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu(x)</annotation></semantics></math> is known. We denote the radius of the label space by <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho(\mathcal{C}):=\max_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\|c\|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi></mrow></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho(\mathcal{C}):=\max_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\|c\|</annotation></semantics></math>. Given a finite hypothesis class <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}</annotation></semantics></math>, our goal is to identify a predictive model <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h\in\mathcal{H}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h\in\mathcal{H}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}</annotation></semantics></math> that minimizes the expected decision loss. Throughout the paper, we assume that <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}</annotation></semantics></math> is finite with cardinality at most <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\mathcal{H}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\mathcal{H}|</annotation></semantics></math>, a standard assumption in experimental design; see, e.g., <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao (2024)</a></cite>. When <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}</annotation></semantics></math> is infinite, our analysis extends by replacing <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\mathcal{H}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\mathcal{H}|</annotation></semantics></math> with a complexity measure such as a covering number; see, e.g., <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wainwright (2019)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In contextual stochastic linear optimization, there is a downstream decision-making problem whereby, given each feature <math id="S1.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, we aim to find a decision <math id="S1.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>w</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w</annotation></semantics></math> that minimizes the conditional expected cost:</p>
<table id="S1.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S1.E1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S1.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\min_{w\in S}\mathbb{E}[c^{\top}w|x]=\min_{w\in S}\mathbb{E}[c^{\top}|x]w," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><munder><mi>min</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></munder><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><munder><mi>min</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></munder><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\min_{w\in S}\mathbb{E}[c^{\top}w|x]=\min_{w\in S}\mathbb{E}[c^{\top}|x]w,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S1.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S1.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the polyhedral feasible region.
We assume that the feasible region <math id="S1.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math> is bounded and define its diameter as <math id="S1.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta(\mathcal{S}):=\sup_{w_{1},w_{2}\in\mathcal{S}}\|w_{1}-w_{2}\|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.1389em">:=</mo><mrow><msub><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0em">sup</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta(\mathcal{S}):=\sup_{w_{1},w_{2}\in\mathcal{S}}\|w_{1}-w_{2}\|</annotation></semantics></math>. Let <math id="S1.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w^{*}(\hat{c}):=\arg\min_{w\in S}\hat{c}^{\top}w" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>w</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>min</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w^{*}(\hat{c}):=\arg\min_{w\in S}\hat{c}^{\top}w</annotation></semantics></math> denote an oracle for solving Problem (<a href="#S1.E1" title="Equation 1 ‣ 1.1 Sequential Design for Predict-then-Optimize ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) under the predicted cost vector <math id="S1.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{c}</annotation></semantics></math>. For simplicity, when Problem (<a href="#S1.E1" title="Equation 1 ‣ 1.1 Sequential Design for Predict-then-Optimize ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) has multiple optimal solutions, we use a consistent tie-breaking rule (e.g., ordering extreme points of the polyhedron), thus the oracle <math id="S1.SS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>w</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> yields a unique solution for every input cost vector <math id="S1.SS1.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>. To quantify the decision loss in the downstream linear optimization, we adopt the Smart Predict-then-Optimize (SPO) loss introduced in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Elmachtoub and Grigas (2022)</a></cite>, defined by</p>
<table id="S1.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S1.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{\textnormal{SPO}}(\hat{c},c)=c^{\top}w^{*}(\hat{c})-c^{\top}w^{*}(c)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mtext>SPO</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>w</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>w</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{\textnormal{SPO}}(\hat{c},c)=c^{\top}w^{*}(\hat{c})-c^{\top}w^{*}(c).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S1.SS1.p3.3" class="ltx_p">Intuitively, the SPO loss quantifies the difference between the cost induced by <math id="S1.SS1.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w^{*}(\hat{c})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>w</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w^{*}(\hat{c})</annotation></semantics></math> and the optimal decision <math id="S1.SS1.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w^{*}(c)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>w</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w^{*}(c)</annotation></semantics></math>, given that the actual cost vector is <math id="S1.SS1.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>.
The SPO risk is defined as the expectation of the SPO loss, i.e., <math id="S1.SS1.p3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\textnormal{SPO}}(h):=\mathbb{E}_{(x,c)\sim\mathcal{D}}[\ell_{\textnormal{SPO}}(h(x),c)]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>SPO</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∼</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mtext>SPO</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\textnormal{SPO}}(h):=\mathbb{E}_{(x,c)\sim\mathcal{D}}[\ell_{\textnormal{SPO}}(h(x),c)]</annotation></semantics></math>. Then, for a given hypothesis class <math id="S1.SS1.p3.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}</annotation></semantics></math>, our goal is to identify a predictive model that minimizes the SPO risk: <math id="S1.SS1.p3.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\min_{h\in\mathcal{H}}R_{\textnormal{SPO}}(h)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>min</mi><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>SPO</mtext></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\min_{h\in\mathcal{H}}R_{\textnormal{SPO}}(h)</annotation></semantics></math>.
Let <math id="S1.SS1.p3.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the set of predictors that achieve the minimum SPO risk, and let <math id="S1.SS1.p3.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{*}\in\mathcal{H}^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{*}\in\mathcal{H}^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> represent one such optimal predictor.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">For convenience, we further introduce the following notations. For the given hypothesis class <math id="S1.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}</annotation></semantics></math>, we use <math id="S1.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathcal{C}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathcal{C}}</annotation></semantics></math> to denote the range of the predicted labels, namely, <math id="S1.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\hat{\mathcal{C}}:=\{c\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:c=h(x),\text{ for some }x\in\mathcal{X}\text{ and }h\in\mathcal{H}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mtext> for some </mtext><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mtext> and </mtext><mi>h</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathcal{C}}:=\{c\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:c=h(x),\text{ for some }x\in\mathcal{X}\text{ and }h\in\mathcal{H}\}</annotation></semantics></math>. We define the maximum SPO loss by <math id="S1.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\omega_{\ell_{\textnormal{SPO}}}(\mathcal{\hat{C}},\mathcal{C}):=\sup_{\hat{c}\in\hat{C},c\in\mathcal{C}}\ell_{\textnormal{SPO}}(\hat{c},c)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>ω</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mtext>SPO</mtext></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.1389em">:=</mo><mrow><msub><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0.167em">sup</mo><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>∈</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mtext>SPO</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\omega_{\ell_{\textnormal{SPO}}}(\mathcal{\hat{C}},\mathcal{C}):=\sup_{\hat{c}\in\hat{C},c\in\mathcal{C}}\ell_{\textnormal{SPO}}(\hat{c},c)</annotation></semantics></math>. We further define <math id="S1.SS1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma:=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\max_{h_{1},h_{2}\in\mathcal{H}}\left\|\frac{h_{1}(x_{i})}{\|h_{1}(x_{i})\|}-\frac{h_{2}(x_{i})}{\|h_{2}(x_{i})\|}\right\|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo rspace="0.111em">:=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi></mrow></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma:=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\max_{h_{1},h_{2}\in\mathcal{H}}\left\|\frac{h_{1}(x_{i})}{\|h_{1}(x_{i})\|}-\frac{h_{2}(x_{i})}{\|h_{2}(x_{i})\|}\right\|</annotation></semantics></math>, as the cumulative maximum directional difference across the hypothesis class for each design.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, the sequential design process is as follows.
At the beginning of iteration <math id="S1.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, we select a candidate design <math id="S1.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}\in\mathcal{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}\in\mathcal{X}</annotation></semantics></math> and conduct an experiment to observe its outcome <math id="S1.SS1.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. Based on this new information from <math id="S1.SS1.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, we then shrink the hypothesis class <math id="S1.SS1.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> to remove some suboptimal prediction models <math id="S1.SS1.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> from <math id="S1.SS1.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. At the end of iteration <math id="S1.SS1.p5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, the best model from the remaining hypothesis class <math id="S1.SS1.p5.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is selected as the output.</p>
</div>

-96.47)"><g class="ltx_tikzmatrix" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 35.42)"><g class="ltx_tikzmatrix_row" transform="matrix(1 0 0 1 0 13.84)"><g class="ltx_tikzmatrix_col ltx_nopad_r" transform="matrix(1 width="268"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S1.F1.pic1.18" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:144%;">Output the best model </span><math id="S1.F1.pic1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathsize="1.440em">h</mi><mi mathsize="1.440em">t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S1.F1.pic1.19" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:144%;"> within</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g><g class="ltx_tikzmatrix_row" transform="matrix(1 0 0 1 0 31.55)"><g class="ltx_tikzmatrix_col ltx_nopad_r" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 6.92 0)"><foreignObject class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S1.F1.pic1.20" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:144%;">the current hypothesis class </span><math id="S1.F1.pic1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathsize="1.440em">H</mi><mi mathsize="1.440em">t</mi></msub><annotation -21.07"></path><g stroke-dasharray="none" stroke-dashoffset="0.0pt" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" transform="matrix(0.0 1.0 -1.0 0.0 415.19 -20.52)"><path style="fill:none" d="M -3.54 -0.5 -2.9 -1.73 -3.54 -4.32"></path></g></g><g stroke-width="0.8pt"><path style="fill:none" d="M 1067.22 -60.03 L 1067.22 -21.77"></path><g stroke-dasharray="none" stroke-dashoffset="0.0pt" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" transform="matrix(0.0 1.0 -1.0 0.0 1067.22 -21.22)"><path style="fill:none" d="M -3.54 4.32 C -2.9 1.73 -1.45 0.5 0 0 C -1.45 -0.5 -2.9 -1.73 -3.54 -4.32"></path></g></g></g></svg></span>
</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span>Illustration of Sequential Experimental Design.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">In Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1.1 Sequential Design for Predict-then-Optimize ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, at each iteration, when selecting design <math id="S1.SS1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, the high-level idea is to find a good metric to evaluate the uncertainty of each design <math id="S1.SS1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>. Intuitively, among the remaining set of potential optimal prediction models <math id="S1.SS1.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h\in H_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h\in H_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, if the uncertainty (disagreement) of the prediction, <math id="S1.SS1.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h(x)</annotation></semantics></math>, is small, then this design <math id="S1.SS1.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> has less contribution to the model elimination, and thus is less likely to be selected.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">An important question is which metric should be used to quantify uncertainty. For a given design <math id="S1.SS1.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and a class of candidate prediction models <math id="S1.SS1.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math>, we compare the following three uncertainty metrics at <math id="S1.SS1.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<ol id="S1.I2" class="ltx_enumerate" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:3em;">
<li id="S1.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S1.I2.i1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Metric 1.</span></span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S1.I2.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\max_{h_{1},h_{2}\in H}\left\{\|h_{1}(x)-h_{2}(x)\|\right\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\max_{h_{1},h_{2}\in H}\left\{\|h_{1}(x)-h_{2}(x)\|\right\}</annotation></semantics></math>  (decision-blind)</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S1.I2.i2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Metric 2.</span></span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S1.I2.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\max_{h_{1},h_{2}\in H}\left|\ell_{\textnormal{SPO}}\!\big(h_{1}(x),h_{2}(x)\big)\right|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>|</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mtext>SPO</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\max_{h_{1},h_{2}\in H}\left|\ell_{\textnormal{SPO}}\!\big(h_{1}(x),h_{2}(x)\big)\right|</annotation></semantics></math>  (computationally intractable)</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S1.I2.i3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Metric 3.</span></span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S1.I2.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\max_{h_{1},h_{2}\in H}\left\{\left\|\frac{h_{1}(x)}{\|h_{1}(x)\|}-\frac{h_{2}(x)}{\|h_{2}(x)\|}\right\|\right\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\max_{h_{1},h_{2}\in H}\left\{\left\|\frac{h_{1}(x)}{\|h_{1}(x)\|}-\frac{h_{2}(x)}{\|h_{2}(x)\|}\right\|\right\}</annotation></semantics></math>  (directional)</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Although <span id="S1.SS1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Metric 1</span> (based on the <math id="S1.SS1.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> norm) is widely used in sequential data collection (e.g., <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sugiyama and Nakajima (2009)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Beygelzimer et al. (2009)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cai et al. (2016)</a></cite>), it may be poorly aligned with the SPO loss (see Example <a href="#S2.Thmtheorem1" title="Example 2.1 ‣ 2.1 Algorithm Motivation ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>). In contrast, <span id="S1.SS1.p8.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Metric 2</span> measures uncertainty directly in terms of the SPO loss, but it is typically computationally prohibitive: evaluating <math id="S1.SS1.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{\textnormal{SPO}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mtext>SPO</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{\textnormal{SPO}}</annotation></semantics></math> requires solving the downstream optimization problem for each predicted cost vector, and quantifying uncertainty over a large set of candidate predictions can require a very large number of optimization-oracle calls. While prior work (e.g., <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2023)</a></cite>) proposes margin-based surrogates to approximate such uncertainty via upper bounds, these approaches still rely on repeatedly solving the optimization problem and can remain computationally expensive.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Motivated by these considerations, we propose <span id="S1.SS1.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Metric 3</span> and show that normalizing predictions yields an uncertainty measure that is both computationally efficient and more closely aligned with the SPO loss. Intuitively, this directional uncertainty discards the scale information in the predictions, which is appropriate because the SPO loss is scale-invariant (see Fact <a href="#Thmthm1" title="Fact 1 (Fact 1: The SPO loss is scale invariant.) ‣ 2.1 Algorithm Motivation ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS1.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.p10.1" class="ltx_p">Before presenting our sequential data collection policy, we illustrate one application of the proposed sequential design in job assignment in Section <a href="#S1.SS2" title="1.2 Application Example: Contextual Job Assignment ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">1.2 </span>Application Example: Contextual Job Assignment</h3>

<div id="S1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider a job assignment problem in which <math id="S1.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> jobs must be assigned to <math id="S1.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> agents to minimize total cost. Let <math id="S1.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{i,j}\in\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{i,j}\in\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math> indicate whether job <math id="S1.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> is assigned to agent <math id="S1.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>, and let <math id="S1.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{i,j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{i,j}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the random cost of assigning job <math id="S1.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> to agent <math id="S1.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>, which depends on contextual information <math id="S1.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>. The problem can be formulated as</p>
<table id="S1.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S1.E4"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
