<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S1.E4.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{i,j}=B_{i},\quad\forall i=1,\dots,m," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo></mstyle><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup><mi>w</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{i,j}=B_{i},\quad\forall i=1,\dots,m,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S1.E5"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S1.E5.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle w_{i,j}\in\{0,1\},\quad\forall i=1,\dots,m,\ j=1,\dots,n." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo rspace="0.667em">,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle w_{i,j}\in\{0,1\},\quad\forall i=1,\dots,m,\ j=1,\dots,n.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S1.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Constraint (<a href="#S1.E3" title="Equation 3 ‣ 1.2 Application Example: Contextual Job Assignment ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>) captures agent capacity limits, while (<a href="#S1.E4" title="Equation 4 ‣ 1.2 Application Example: Contextual Job Assignment ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) ensures that each job’s demand is satisfied.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A motivating specific problem is LLM task allocation. Different LLMs exhibit heterogeneous performance across tasks and incur different computational costs. When computational resources are limited, it is desirable to assign more complex tasks to high-capacity models and simpler tasks to lightweight models. In this setting, <math id="S1.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the number of tasks, <math id="S1.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> the number of available LLMs, <math id="S1.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> the task or document type, and <math id="S1.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{i,j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{i,j}</annotation></semantics></math> the (negative) performance score of model <math id="S1.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> on task <math id="S1.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>. The assignment decision <math id="S1.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>w</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w</annotation></semantics></math> is obtained by solving Problem (<a href="#S1.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ 1.2 Application Example: Contextual Job Assignment ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), where <math id="S1.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> represents the processing capacity of model <math id="S1.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S1.SS2.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{i}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{i}=1</annotation></semantics></math> for all <math id="S1.SS2.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In the above example, building the prediction model requires a training set with labeled samples, and obtaining this training set can be costly (e.g., human evaluation of the performance of LLMs on processed tasks). Hence, it is important to apply an efficient data collection algorithm.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">1.3 </span>Related Work</h3>

<div id="S1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To position our paper, we summarize some related work in decision-focused learning and sequential experimental design.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Decision-focused learning and contextual optimization</span>. Contextual optimization studies how to use contextual features to estimate uncertain parameters in optimization. In the predict-then-optimize regime, where point predictions of the uncertain parameters are used directly, higher predictive accuracy does not necessarily yield a smaller decision loss. Decision-focused learning (DFL), therefore, incorporates the downstream decision-making problem into the training of prediction models. Given the large and growing literature, we cite a representative subset of works most relevant to our linear optimization setting and refer readers to surveys such as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mandi et al. (2024)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sadana et al. (2025)</a></cite> for additional references and broader perspectives.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bertsimas and Kallus (2020)</a></cite> uses local prediction models to estimate the downstream decision loss. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al. (2022)</a></cite> considers the joint estimation and optimization from a robust perspective. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Er and Liu (2025)</a></cite> further addresses the necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of the decision-unbiased predictions for linear optimization.
A stream of research by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Donti et al. (2017)</a></cite> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Amos and Kolter (2017)</a></cite> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mandi et al. (2020)</a></cite> applied implicit differentiation to perform gradient updates on the prediction model parameters. Another stream of research is to use an analytical surrogate loss function that can be differentiated through. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Elmachtoub and Grigas (2022)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang and Gupta (2024)</a></cite> propose different surrogate loss functions and establish their consistency under various conditions. Other related DFL methods include <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chung et al. (2022)</a></cite>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feng and Shanthikumar (2022)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feng et al. (2025)</a></cite>, and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cristian et al. (2025)</a></cite>. In the context of data collection for predict-then-optimize, the sample complexity and generalization error bounds developed in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ho-Nguyen and Kılınç-Karzan (2022)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">El Balghiti et al. (2022)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al. (2022)</a></cite> can be used to derive stopping-time guarantees for data collection. Although the motivation for DFL is clear, theoretically establishing its statistical benefit is nontrivial; see, for example, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al. (2022)</a></cite>. A stream of papers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Elmachtoub et al. (2023)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Elmachtoub et al. (2025)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lan et al. (2025)</a></cite> studies this benefit relative to the two-stage approach under model misspecification.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The above works on decision-focused learning either assume that the data are given a priori or that they are collected in an i.i.d. manner. In contrast, our paper is the first to study the SPO loss in a sequential experimental design setting with noisy observations, where the data collected are inherently non-i.i.d. Moreover, our paper is the first to demonstrate a statistical benefit of DFL over decision-blind design under specific structural assumptions on the noise distributions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sequential Experimental Design</span>. Experimental design has a long history in statistics and operations research. Classical work develops optimality criteria (e.g., A-, D-, and E-optimality) and studies structured designs such as Box–Behnken; see, e.g., <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1959)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Box and Behnken (1960)</a></cite>. These ideas have broad applications in physical and engineering experiments. More recently, sequential and adaptive procedures select the next experiment based on the data collected so far, resulting in stagewise designs that improve sample efficiency; see, for example, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anderer et al. (2022)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Che et al. (2024)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao and Zhou (2025)</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li (2025)</a></cite>. In regression settings, a closely related line of work—often discussed under the name <em id="S1.SS3.p4.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">pool-based selective sampling</em>—studies policies that sequentially select which inputs to label to improve a predictor efficiently <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Castro et al. 2005</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sugiyama and Nakajima 2009</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cai et al. 2016</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Beygelzimer et al. 2009</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al. 2025</a>)</cite>. These methods can be viewed as sequential design rules in which the <em id="S1.SS3.p4.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">information value</em> of a candidate point is scored, and labels are acquired accordingly. Within this stream, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Beygelzimer et al. (2009)</a></cite> propose an importance-weighted algorithm (IWAL) that generalizes classification algorithms to regressions. IWAL measures, for a candidate feature vector, the maximum difference in loss over all possible labels and uses that quantity to set a sampling probability. While elegant, computing these scores becomes challenging when the loss departs from squared error, limiting direct applicability in decision-oriented contexts.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In the decision-focused setting, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bennouna et al. (2025)</a></cite> consider the offline data collection problem in a noiseless setting. To incorporate the SPO loss into the sequential data collection process, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2023)</a></cite> develop a margin-based sequential design using the notion of <em id="S1.SS3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">distance to degeneracy</em>. They show theoretical and empirical gains by utilizing the distances to the margins. However, their approach assumes access to margin information, which is computationally demanding when the feasible region is complex, and it treats near-degenerate points uniformly without distinguishing their relative information values.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">In contrast, our sequential experimental design is computationally tractable by targeting <em id="S1.SS3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">directional uncertainty</em>. Conceptually, our work bridges classical sequential experimental design and decision-focused learning by tailoring information gathering to task structure.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Algorithm and Performance Guarantees</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we motivate the proposed uncertainty metric and present the corresponding algorithm. We then establish theoretical performance guarantees under mild assumptions.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Algorithm Motivation</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In sequential experimental design problems, a common approach is to use prediction uncertainty to determine the next design sequentially. At each step, we aim to observe the outcome of an experiment whose predictive distribution has high uncertainty, rather than an experiment that the model has already learned well. A typical method for quantifying prediction uncertainty is to use the <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> distance among the predictions produced by all hypotheses. However, this <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> based criterion is decision-blind, and hence, when considering the SPO loss, it may lead to inefficiency in the predict-then-optimize setting.
To illustrate why a standard distance metric may fail to align with the SPO loss, let us consider the following example in Figure <a href="#S2.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 2.1 Algorithm Motivation ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F3" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S2.F3.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_top" style="width:138.0pt;"><img src="2602.05340v1/illus_3_1.png" id="S2.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:191/207;" width="191" height="207" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F3.fig1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S2.F3.fig1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Cost Vector Prediction with Corresponding Optimizer</span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S2.F3.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_top" style="width:165.6pt;"><img src="2602.05340v1/illus_3_2.png" id="S2.F3.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:229/192;" width="229" height="192" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F3.fig2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S2.F3.fig2.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Cost Vector Prediction with <math id="S2.F3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> Distance</span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_example">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Example 2.1</span></span></h6>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Consider a two-dimensional setting where the current hypothesis class contains two predictors <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}=\{h_{1},h_{2}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}=\{h_{1},h_{2}\}</annotation></semantics></math>. Suppose there are two designs <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{X}=\{x_{1},x_{2}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{X}=\{x_{1},x_{2}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, denoted by red (<math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>) and green (<math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>) dots respectively in Figure <a href="#S2.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 2.1 Algorithm Motivation ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. Let <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{1}(x_{1}),h_{1}(x_{2}),h_{2}(x_{1}),h_{2}(x_{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{1}(x_{1}),h_{1}(x_{2}),h_{2}(x_{1}),h_{2}(x_{2})</annotation></semantics></math> denote the corresponding predictions. Figure <a href="#S2.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 2.1 Algorithm Motivation ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows the feasible region <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math>, predicted cost vectors, and their corresponding optimizers. For ease of illustration, we represent each cost vector by its negative direction. Because of the linearity of the objective function, the optimal solution corresponds to the vertex of the cone containing the predicted cost vector. To evaluate the uncertainty of the two possible designs, Figure <a href="#S2.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 2.1 Algorithm Motivation ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows the location of prediction values and the area of predictions that corresponds to the optimality of each vertex. In Figure <a href="#S2.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 2.1 Algorithm Motivation ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, although the size of the green circle is larger, indicating that <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}</annotation></semantics></math> exhibits greater <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> uncertainty on <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> than on <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>, the predictions at <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> yield the same optimizer. Thus, the uncertainty of SPO loss on <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is zero. On the other hand, the predictions of <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{1}(x_{1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{1}(x_{1})</annotation></semantics></math> result in a different optimizer from <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{2}(x_{1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{2}(x_{1})</annotation></semantics></math>. It implies that the uncertainty of SPO loss on <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> is nonzero. Hence, from the perspective of the SPO loss, <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> has a larger uncertainty, even though <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> exhibits a larger <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> uncertainty.  <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\square" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">□</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\square</annotation></semantics></math></span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Example <a href="#S2.Thmtheorem1" title="Example 2.1 ‣ 2.1 Algorithm Motivation ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a> shows that there may exist a misalignment between decision-focused uncertainty and <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> distance. This misalignment is due to a scale-invariant property of SPO loss, as pointed out by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Elmachtoub and Grigas (2022)</a></cite> and stated in the following fact.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmthm1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_fact">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmthm1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Fact 1</span></span><span id="Thmthm1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Fact 1: The SPO loss is scale invariant.)</h6>
<div id="Thmthm1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmthm1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmthm1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">For all <math id="Thmthm1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{c}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Thmthm1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, it holds that <math id="Thmthm1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w^{*}(\hat{c})=w^{*}(\alpha\hat{c})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>w</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>w</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w^{*}(\hat{c})=w^{*}(\alpha\hat{c})</annotation></semantics></math>. Consequently, we have <math id="Thmthm1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{\textnormal{SPO}}(\alpha\hat{c},c)=\ell_{\textnormal{SPO}}(\hat{c},c)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mtext>SPO</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mtext>SPO</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{\textnormal{SPO}}(\alpha\hat{c},c)=\ell_{\textnormal{SPO}}(\hat{c},c)</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Fact <a href="#Thmthm1" title="Fact 1 (Fact 1: The SPO loss is scale invariant.) ‣ 2.1 Algorithm Motivation ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> shows that for a fixed true cost vector <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{\textnormal{SPO}}(\cdot,c)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mtext>SPO</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{\textnormal{SPO}}(\cdot,c)</annotation></semantics></math> is scale invariant in the prediction <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{c}</annotation></semantics></math>.
This motivates us to utilize directional information to quantify predictive uncertainty. Accordingly, we propose a directional uncertainty metric that better aligns with the SPO loss while remaining tractable; see Figure <a href="#S2.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 2.1 Algorithm Motivation ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> (vs. the standard <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> metric in Figure <a href="#S2.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 2.1 Algorithm Motivation ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F5" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S2.F5.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_top" style="width:138.0pt;"><img src="2602.05340v1/illustration_2.png" id="S2.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:191/141;" width="191" height="141" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F5.fig1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><math id="S2.F5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em" mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S2.F5.fig1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> Based Uncertainty</span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S2.F5.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_top" style="width:138.0pt;"><img src="2602.05340v1/illustration_1.png" id="S2.F5.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:191/141;" width="191" height="141" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F5.fig2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S2.F5.fig2.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Direction-Based Uncertainty</span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In Figures <a href="#S2.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 2.1 Algorithm Motivation ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> and <a href="#S2.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 2.1 Algorithm Motivation ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, there are three possible designs (represented by red, green, and blue colors of dots) and four candidate prediction models, <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{1},...,h_{4}\in\mathcal{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{1},...,h_{4}\in\mathcal{H}</annotation></semantics></math>. We assume the target cost vector <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c\in\mathbb{R}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c\in\mathbb{R}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> has two dimensions, and each dot indicates a model’s predicted cost vector for a given design. The circle stands for the maximum <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> distance among the predictions for these three designs. Based on the sizes of the circles in Figure <a href="#S2.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 2.1 Algorithm Motivation ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, the green design has the largest uncertainty and thus should be most likely to be selected by a standard approach. However, based on our new directional uncertainty in Figure <a href="#S2.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 2.1 Algorithm Motivation ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, the red design has the largest angle difference, and thus is most likely to be selected, correctly reflecting the decision-focused nature of the problem.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Importance Weighted Sequential Experimental Design</h3>

             <span id="alg1.l1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Input:</span>

             Set <math id="alg1.l2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{0}\leftarrow\emptyset" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∅</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{0}\leftarrow\emptyset</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="alg1.l2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{0}\leftarrow 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{0}\leftarrow 0</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="alg1.l2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{0}\leftarrow\mathcal{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{0}\leftarrow\mathcal{H}</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l4" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">4:</span></span>
              
              
              For each potential design <math id="alg1.l4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{X}_{(i)}\in\mathcal{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo encoding="application/x-tex">p_{t,i}=\max_{h_{1},h_{2}\in H_{t}}\left\{\left\|\frac{h_{1}(\mathrm{X}_{(i)})}{\|h_{1}(\mathrm{X}_{(i)})\|}-\frac{h_{2}(\mathrm{X}_{(i)})}{\|h_{2}(\mathrm{X}_{(i)})\|}\right\|\right\}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="alg1.l4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{t,i}\leftarrow\frac{p_{t,i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{m}p_{t,j}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{t,i}\leftarrow\frac{p_{t,i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{m}p_{t,j}}</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l5" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">5:</span></span>

<div id="alg1.l14" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l14.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">14:</span></span>
              
              
              Update the confidence set of the predictor <math id="alg1.l14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> by <math id="alg1.l14.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{t}\leftarrow\{h\in H_{t-1}:\hat{\ell}^{t}(h)\leq\hat{\ell}^{t,*}+r_{t}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mo lspace="0em">∗</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{t}\leftarrow\{h\in H_{t-1}:\hat{\ell}^{t}(h)\leq\hat{\ell}^{t,*}+r_{t}\}</annotation></semantics></math>

              Update <math id="alg1.l15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{t+1}\leftarrow r_{t}\sqrt{\frac{t}{t+1}\frac{\log(2(t+1))}{\log(2t)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{t+1}\leftarrow r_{t}\sqrt{\frac{t}{t+1}\frac{\log(2(t+1))}{\log(2t)}}</annotation></semantics></math>

             <span id="alg1.l17.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Return</span> <math id="alg1.l17.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{T}</annotation></semantics></math>

</figure>
<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our importance-weighted sequential design algorithm based on directional uncertainty (IWSD-DU) is stated in Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ 2.2 Importance Weighted Sequential Experimental Design ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. The algorithm operates in a sequential design environment where, at the beginning of each iteration <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, we can actively select a sample <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> from the pool <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathcal{X}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathcal{X}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The algorithm maintains a confidence set of predictors <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>⊆</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{H}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Initially, the confidence set of the predictor is set as the entire hypothesis space <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}</annotation></semantics></math>. To obtain the sample weights in each period, we calculate the maximum <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> norm of prediction difference for the predictors within the current confidence set <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. In this step, calculating the labeling probability is computationally easy, especially when the confidence set <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> contains a finite number of predictors.
To determine which design point to query, we sample <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}=\mathrm{X}_{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}=\mathrm{X}_{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math> with probability <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{t,i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{t,i}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{t,i}=\frac{p_{t,i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{m}p_{t,j}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="false"><msubsup><mo maxsize="0.700em" minsize="0.700em" stretchy="true">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></msubsup></mstyle><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{t,i}=\frac{p_{t,i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{m}p_{t,j}}</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="S2.SS2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{t,i}=\max_{h_{1},h_{2}\in H_{t}}\left\{\left\|\frac{h_{1}(x_{i})}{\|h_{1}(x_{i})\|}-\frac{h_{2}(x_{i})}{\|h_{2}(x_{i})\|}\right\|\right\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{t,i}=\max_{h_{1},h_{2}\in H_{t}}\left\{\left\|\frac{h_{1}(x_{i})}{\|h_{1}(x_{i})\|}-\frac{h_{2}(x_{i})}{\|h_{2}(x_{i})\|}\right\|\right\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Intuitively, <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{t,i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{t,i}</annotation></semantics></math> measures the maximum directional disagreement in the predicted cost vector at <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> among all hypotheses in the current hypothesis class <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. A larger value of <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{t,i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{t,i}</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to greater uncertainty at <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, resulting in a higher sampling probability <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{t,i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{t,i}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For ease of notation, let <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q_{t,i}\in\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_{t,i}\in\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the indicator random variable that equals one if the outcome of <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to feature <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, for all <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i\in[m]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i\in[m]</annotation></semantics></math>, that is, <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="Q_{t,i}\leftarrow\mathbb{I}\{x_{t}=\mathrm{X}_{(i)}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mi>𝕀</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_{t,i}\leftarrow\mathbb{I}\{x_{t}=\mathrm{X}_{(i)}\}</annotation></semantics></math>. After designing an experiment <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, we observe an outcome <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> drawn from the conditional distribution of <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> given <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and add the sample <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x_{t},c_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x_{t},c_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> and its corresponding weight <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{t,i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{t,i}</annotation></semantics></math> into the existing training set <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{t-1}</annotation></semantics></math>.
After each iteration, we update the prediction model by minimizing the empirical re-weighted loss, which is defined as</p>
</div>

<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><span id="S2.Ex2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath">if design <math id="S2.Ex2.m2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is chosen.</span></td>

<div id="S2.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ 2.2 Importance Weighted Sequential Experimental Design ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, the random variables at iteration <math id="S2.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> are <math id="S2.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x_{t},c_{t},\pi_{t},Q_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x_{t},c_{t},\pi_{t},Q_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">With slight abuse of notation, in Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ 2.2 Importance Weighted Sequential Experimental Design ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, the re-weighted loss function at iteration <math id="S2.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> can be rewritten as</p>
</div>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">In Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ 2.2 Importance Weighted Sequential Experimental Design ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, the confidence set for the optimal prediction models is constructed by allowing a slackness <math id="S2.SS2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> of the empirical reweighted loss, compared to the current minimum empirical loss. Specifically, <math id="S2.SS2.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{t}\leftarrow\{h\in H_{t-1}:\hat{\ell}^{t}(h)\leq\hat{\ell}^{t,*}+r_{t}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mo lspace="0em">∗</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{t}\leftarrow\{h\in H_{t-1}:\hat{\ell}^{t}(h)\leq\hat{\ell}^{t,*}+r_{t}\}</annotation></semantics></math>. Because this confidence set is nested, the directional uncertainty <math id="S2.SS2.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{t,i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{t,i}</annotation></semantics></math> associated with each design <math id="S2.SS2.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is nonincreasing in <math id="S2.SS2.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. As the number of observations <math id="S2.SS2.p7.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> grows sufficiently large, the directional uncertainties of all designs approach zero, which induces a stopping time for the sequential experimental design.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Preliminaries for Theoretical Guarantees</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this subsection, we discuss the preliminaries for our algorithm’s theoretical guarantees. For simplicity, we use random variable <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="z_{t}\in\mathcal{Z}:=\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{C}\times(0,1]^{m}\times\{0,1\}^{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒵</mi><mo>:=</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}\in\mathcal{Z}:=\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{C}\times(0,1]^{m}\times\{0,1\}^{m}</annotation></semantics></math> to denote the tuple of random variables <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}:=(x_{t},c_{t},\pi_{t},Q_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}:=(x_{t},c_{t},\pi_{t},Q_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>. Thus, <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> depends on <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{1},...,z_{t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{1},...,z_{t-1}</annotation></semantics></math> and thus is non i.i.d.. We define <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{t-1}</annotation></semantics></math> as the <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>-field of all random variables until the end of iteration <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t-1</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e., <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{1},...,z_{t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{1},...,z_{t-1}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Given the sampling probability <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{t}=(\pi_{t,1},\dots,\pi_{t,m})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{t}=(\pi_{t,1},\dots,\pi_{t,m})</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q_{t}=(Q_{t,1},\dots,Q_{t,m})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_{t}=(Q_{t,1},\dots,Q_{t,m})</annotation></semantics></math> is a random vector that is independent of other randomness and <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}[Q_{t,i}]=\pi_{t,i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}[Q_{t,i}]=\pi_{t,i}</annotation></semantics></math>, the expectation of the re-weighted loss is</p>
<table id="S2.EGx5" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.Ex4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}[\frac{\mu(x_{i})}{\pi_{t,i}}Q_{t,i}\ell_{\textnormal{SPO}}(h(x_{i}),c_{i})]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover></mstyle><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mtext>SPO</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}[\frac{\mu(x_{i})}{\pi_{t,i}}Q_{t,i}\ell_{\textnormal{SPO}}(h(x_{i}),c_{i})]</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
