</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This implies that the expectation of the re-weighted loss is an unbiased estimator for the risk of <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>. Thus, under certain assumptions (Assumption <a href="#S2.SS3" title="2.3 Preliminaries for Theoretical Guarantees ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a>), the empirical re-weighted loss is expected to converge to the risk, and its minimizer <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> over the confidence set <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}_{t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}_{t-1}</annotation></semantics></math> is expected to converge to the true SPO risk minimizer <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To establish convergence, as shown in the proof of Theorem <a href="#S2.Thmtheorem5" title="Theorem 2.5 (Risk Bound) ‣ 2.4 Risk Bound and Rates ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.5</span></a>, the reweighted loss
<math id="S2.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell^{\mathtt{rew}}(h;(x_{t},c_{t},\pi_{t}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>𝚛𝚎𝚠</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell^{\mathtt{rew}}(h;(x_{t},c_{t},\pi_{t}))</annotation></semantics></math> must admit a uniform upper bound at each iteration. Intuitively, this requirement ensures that when the sampling probability <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is small, the resulting excess SPO loss is proportionally small, which induces a “Lipschitz-like” behavior. Since the SPO loss is not Lipschitz continuous in general, we impose an additional assumption to guarantee this property.
A sufficient condition for this “Lipschitz-like” property is a lower-bound condition on the angle between the predicted cost vector and the degenerate cost vectors. The formal statement of this assumption is provided below, together with the definition of the distance to degeneracy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 2.2</span></span><span id="S2.Thmtheorem2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Distance to Degeneracy, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">El Balghiti et al. (2022)</a></cite>)</h6>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">For a polyhedron <math id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math>, the set of degenerate cost vectors is defined as <math id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}^{o}:=\{\hat{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\min_{w\in\mathcal{S}}\hat{c}^{\top}w\text{ has multiple solutions}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mi>o</mi></msup><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>min</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic"> has multiple solutions</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}^{o}:=\{\hat{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\min_{w\in\mathcal{S}}\hat{c}^{\top}w\text{ has multiple solutions}\}</annotation></semantics></math>. The distance to degeneracy of a prediction <math id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{c}</annotation></semantics></math> is defined as <math id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu_{\mathcal{S}}(\hat{c}):=\inf_{c\in\mathcal{C}^{o}}\{\|c-\hat{c}\|\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>ν</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.1389em">:=</mo><mrow><msub><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0em">inf</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mi>o</mi></msup></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu_{\mathcal{S}}(\hat{c}):=\inf_{c\in\mathcal{C}^{o}}\{\|c-\hat{c}\|\}</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The distance to degeneracy quantifies the largest perturbation of the prediction <math id="S2.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{c}</annotation></semantics></math> that still preserves the optimality of the current decision <math id="S2.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w^{*}(\hat{c})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>w</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w^{*}(\hat{c})</annotation></semantics></math>. If the distance to degeneracy <math id="S2.SS3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu_{\mathcal{S}}(c)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ν</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu_{\mathcal{S}}(c)</annotation></semantics></math> for a cost vector <math id="S2.SS3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> is large, then adding a small noise or slightly perturbing the prediction will not change the optimizer of the downstream problem. On the other hand, if <math id="S2.SS3.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu_{\mathcal{S}}(c)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ν</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu_{\mathcal{S}}(c)</annotation></semantics></math> is relatively small, then perturbing the vector might lead to different solutions in the downstream problem. Hence, for a prediction <math id="S2.SS3.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{c}</annotation></semantics></math>, if <math id="S2.SS3.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu_{\mathcal{S}}(\hat{c})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ν</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu_{\mathcal{S}}(\hat{c})</annotation></semantics></math> is large, then we are more confident about the decision loss incurred by <math id="S2.SS3.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{c}</annotation></semantics></math>.
This distance to degeneracy serves as a key concept in showing the “Lipschitz” property of the SPO loss, as shown in Assumption <a href="#S2.SS3" title="2.3 Preliminaries for Theoretical Guarantees ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para"><span id="S2.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_ERROR undefined">{assumption}</span>
<p id="S2.SS3.p5.2" class="ltx_p">[Directional Margin Condition]

There exists a constant <math id="S2.SS3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> such that for all <math id="S2.SS3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h\in\mathcal{H},x\in\mathcal{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h\in\mathcal{H},x\in\mathcal{X}</annotation></semantics></math>, it holds that <math id="S2.SS3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\nu_{\mathcal{S}}(h(x))}{\|h(x)\|}\geq\eta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>ν</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>≥</mo><mi>η</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\nu_{\mathcal{S}}(h(x))}{\|h(x)\|}\geq\eta</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Assumption <a href="#S2.SS3" title="2.3 Preliminaries for Theoretical Guarantees ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a> is a very mild assumption. Actually, given the set of possible designs <math id="S2.SS3.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{X}</annotation></semantics></math>, all finite hypothesis classes <math id="S2.SS3.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}</annotation></semantics></math> can satisfy Assumption <a href="#S2.SS3" title="2.3 Preliminaries for Theoretical Guarantees ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a> easily with a parameter <math id="S2.SS3.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> by a simple equivalent transformation, as detailed in Section <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Justification of the Directional Margin Condition ‣ 4 Justifications and Examples of Assumptions ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a> later.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_remark">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Remark 2.3</span></span><span id="S2.Thmtheorem3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Geometric Interpretation of Directional Margin Condition.)</h6>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Intuitively, Assumption <a href="#S2.SS3" title="2.3 Preliminaries for Theoretical Guarantees ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a> ensures a lower bound for <math id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\nu_{\mathcal{S}}(h(x))}{\|h(x)\|}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>ν</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\nu_{\mathcal{S}}(h(x))}{\|h(x)\|}</annotation></semantics></math>, which is equivalent to an angular condition, as shown in Figure <a href="#S2.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Remark 2.3 (Geometric Interpretation of Directional Margin Condition.) ‣ 2.3 Preliminaries for Theoretical Guarantees ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>. To illustrate this angle condition, we first observe that the label space <math id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> can be partitioned into multiple normal cones. Specifically, for a bounded polyhedron <math id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math>, there exists a convex hull representation <math id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}=\text{conv}\{v_{1},\dots,v_{k}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">conv</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}=\text{conv}\{v_{1},\dots,v_{k}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{1},\dots,v_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{1},\dots,v_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the vertices of <math id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math>. For each vertex <math id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>, define a cone <math id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{K}_{j}=\{\hat{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:v_{j}=\arg\min_{w\in\mathcal{S}}\hat{c}^{\top}w\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒦</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>min</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{K}_{j}=\{\hat{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:v_{j}=\arg\min_{w\in\mathcal{S}}\hat{c}^{\top}w\}</annotation></semantics></math> to be the corresponding normal cone of the cost vector <math id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{c}</annotation></semantics></math> whose optimizer is <math id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>. (We can assume for each <math id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> there exists only one negative normal cone that contains it by applying the tie-breaking rule we previously assumed). Using this representation, we have <math id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p1.m12" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d}=\cup_{j=1}^{k}\mathcal{K}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ℝ</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>d</mi></msup><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em">∪</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒦</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{d}=\cup_{j=1}^{k}\mathcal{K}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Consequently, for all <math id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h\in\mathcal{H},x\in\mathcal{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h\in\mathcal{H},x\in\mathcal{X}</annotation></semantics></math>, each prediction <math id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h(x)</annotation></semantics></math> lies in a corresponding negative normal cone <math id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{K}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒦</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{K}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>. The boundary of the cone is the degenerate cost vector defined in Definition <a href="#S2.Thmtheorem2" title="Definition 2.2 (Distance to Degeneracy, ( ) ) ‣ 2.3 Preliminaries for Theoretical Guarantees ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>. As shown in Figure <a href="#S2.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Remark 2.3 (Geometric Interpretation of Directional Margin Condition.) ‣ 2.3 Preliminaries for Theoretical Guarantees ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, by some simple trigonometric functions, <math id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\nu_{\mathcal{S}}(h(x))}{\|h(x)\|}\geq\eta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>ν</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>≥</mo><mi>η</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\nu_{\mathcal{S}}(h(x))}{\|h(x)\|}\geq\eta</annotation></semantics></math> is equivalent to</span></p>
<table id="S2.Ex8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left\|\frac{h(x)}{\|h(x)\|}-\frac{c^{o}}{\|c^{o}\|}\right\|\geq 2\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)=2\sin\left(\frac{\arcsin(\eta)}{2}\right),\quad\text{ for all degenerate cost vector }c^{o}\in\mathcal{K}_{j}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msup><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mi>θ</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>arcsin</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>η</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic"> for all degenerate cost vector </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi></msup></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒦</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\|\frac{h(x)}{\|h(x)\|}-\frac{c^{o}}{\|c^{o}\|}\right\|\geq 2\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)=2\sin\left(\frac{\arcsin(\eta)}{2}\right),\quad\text{ for all degenerate cost vector }c^{o}\in\mathcal{K}_{j}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.05340v1/illus_4.png" id="S2.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:286/141;" width="286" height="141" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering ltx_font_italic"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F6.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="S2.F6.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Directional Margin Condition</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">This implies that the lower bound of <math id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\nu_{\mathcal{S}}(h(x))}{\|h(x)\|}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>ν</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\nu_{\mathcal{S}}(h(x))}{\|h(x)\|}</annotation></semantics></math> is equivalent to the lower bound of the angle between <math id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h(x)</annotation></semantics></math> and its closest boundary of the cone that <math id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h(x)</annotation></semantics></math> lies in. <math id="S2.Thmtheorem3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\square" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">□</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\square</annotation></semantics></math></span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">With Assumption <a href="#S2.SS3" title="2.3 Preliminaries for Theoretical Guarantees ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a>, Lemma <a href="#S2.Thmtheorem4" title='Lemma 2.4 (“Lipschitz-like” property of ℓ_"SPO" under directional margin condition) ‣ 2.3 Preliminaries for Theoretical Guarantees ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach' class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4</span></a> shows that the SPO loss has a“Lipchitz” like property.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem4" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_lemma">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lemma 2.4</span></span><span id="S2.Thmtheorem4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(“Lipschitz-like” property of <math id="S2.Thmtheorem4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{\textnormal{SPO}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mtext>SPO</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{\textnormal{SPO}}</annotation></semantics></math> under directional margin condition)</h6>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.Thmtheorem4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Under Assumption <a href="#S2.SS3" title="2.3 Preliminaries for Theoretical Guarantees ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a>, for any <math id="S2.Thmtheorem4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{1},h_{2}\in\mathcal{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{1},h_{2}\in\mathcal{H}</annotation></semantics></math> and any <math id="S2.Thmtheorem4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x,c)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x,c)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{C}</annotation></semantics></math>, there exists a constant <math id="S2.Thmtheorem4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L=\frac{\Delta(\mathcal{S})\rho(\mathcal{C})}{2\eta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mi rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>η</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L=\frac{\Delta(\mathcal{S})\rho(\mathcal{C})}{2\eta}</annotation></semantics></math> such that <math id="S2.Thmtheorem4.p1.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\ell_{\textnormal{SPO}}(.,c)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mtext>SPO</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{\textnormal{SPO}}(.,c)</annotation></semantics></math> is L-Lipchitz with respect to the directional difference, namely,</span></p>

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<div id="S2.SS3.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p8.1" class="ltx_p">The proof of Lemma <a href="#S2.Thmtheorem4" title='Lemma 2.4 (“Lipschitz-like” property of ℓ_"SPO" under directional margin condition) ‣ 2.3 Preliminaries for Theoretical Guarantees ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach' class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4</span></a>, along with the remaining proofs, is provided in the appendix.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.4 </span>Risk Bound and Rates</h3>

<div id="S2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">With the “Lipschitz-like” property established in Lemma <a href="#S2.Thmtheorem4" title='Lemma 2.4 (“Lipschitz-like” property of ℓ_"SPO" under directional margin condition) ‣ 2.3 Preliminaries for Theoretical Guarantees ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach' class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4</span></a>, we are ready to show the convergence of IWSD-DU (Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ 2.2 Importance Weighted Sequential Experimental Design ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) in Theorem <a href="#S2.Thmtheorem5" title="Theorem 2.5 (Risk Bound) ‣ 2.4 Risk Bound and Rates ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.5</span></a>. The high-level idea of the proof is to construct a martingale difference sequence and apply Azuma’s inequality to prove the risk bound under a finite sample guarantee.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem5" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 2.5</span></span><span id="S2.Thmtheorem5.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Risk Bound)</h6>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.Thmtheorem5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Suppose that Assumption <a href="#S2.SS3" title="2.3 Preliminaries for Theoretical Guarantees ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a> holds. Let <math id="S2.Thmtheorem5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta\in(0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta\in(0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> be a given parameter, and set <math id="S2.Thmtheorem5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{0}\leftarrow\max\{2\omega_{\ell}(\hat{\mathcal{C}},\mathcal{C}),2\gamma L\sqrt{\log(2|\mathcal{H}|/\delta)}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ω</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{0}\leftarrow\max\{2\omega_{\ell}(\hat{\mathcal{C}},\mathcal{C}),2\gamma L\sqrt{\log(2|\mathcal{H}|/\delta)}\}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S2.Thmtheorem5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> is the Lipschitz constant in Lemma <a href="#S2.Thmtheorem4" title='Lemma 2.4 (“Lipschitz-like” property of ℓ_"SPO" under directional margin condition) ‣ 2.3 Preliminaries for Theoretical Guarantees ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach' class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4</span></a>. Then, with probability at least <math id="S2.Thmtheorem5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-\delta</annotation></semantics></math>, for all <math id="S2.Thmtheorem5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T\geq 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T\geq 1</annotation></semantics></math>, the SPO risk satisfies</span></p>
<table id="S2.Ex10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\textnormal{SPO}}(h_{T})-R_{\textnormal{SPO}}(h^{*})\leq 4\gamma L\sqrt{\frac{\log(2T|\mathcal{H}|/\delta)}{T}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>SPO</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>SPO</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mfrac><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>T</mi></mfrac></msqrt></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\textnormal{SPO}}(h_{T})-R_{\textnormal{SPO}}(h^{*})\leq 4\gamma L\sqrt{\frac{\log(2T|\mathcal{H}|/\delta)}{T}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In practice, the stopping time for the experimental design is determined by a tolerance for the decision loss, which is denoted by <math id="S2.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math>. Based on Theorem <a href="#S2.Thmtheorem5" title="Theorem 2.5 (Risk Bound) ‣ 2.4 Risk Bound and Rates ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.5</span></a>, we can derive an upper bound for the stopping time for the IWSD-DU under the tolerance <math id="S2.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> in Theorem <a href="#S2.Thmtheorem6" title="Theorem 2.6 (Sample complexity) ‣ 2.4 Risk Bound and Rates ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem6" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 2.6</span></span><span id="S2.Thmtheorem6.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Sample complexity)</h6>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.Thmtheorem6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Under the assumption of Theorem <a href="#S2.Thmtheorem5" title="Theorem 2.5 (Risk Bound) ‣ 2.4 Risk Bound and Rates ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.5</span></a>, given any <math id="S2.Thmtheorem6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.Thmtheorem6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta\in(0,1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta\in(0,1)</annotation></semantics></math>, define
<math id="S2.Thmtheorem6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau:=\frac{3(4\gamma L)^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\log\frac{2|\mathcal{H}|}{\epsilon^{2}\delta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><msup><mi>ϵ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>ϵ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau:=\frac{3(4\gamma L)^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\log\frac{2|\mathcal{H}|}{\epsilon^{2}\delta}</annotation></semantics></math>. We have that <math id="S2.Thmtheorem6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\forall T\geq\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\forall T\geq\tau</annotation></semantics></math>, with probability <math id="S2.Thmtheorem6.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-\delta</annotation></semantics></math>, we have <math id="S2.Thmtheorem6.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\textnormal{SPO}}(h_{T})-R_{\textnormal{SPO}}(h^{*})\leq\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>SPO</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>SPO</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\textnormal{SPO}}(h_{T})-R_{\textnormal{SPO}}(h^{*})\leq\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The stopping time <math id="S2.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> characterized in Theorem <a href="#S2.Thmtheorem6" title="Theorem 2.6 (Sample complexity) ‣ 2.4 Risk Bound and Rates ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.6</span></a> provides explicit control over the number of design points queried. By combining this stopping-time with the risk bound from Theorem <a href="#S2.Thmtheorem5" title="Theorem 2.5 (Risk Bound) ‣ 2.4 Risk Bound and Rates ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.5</span></a>, we obtain Proposition <a href="#S2.Thmtheorem7" title="Proposition 2.7 ‣ 2.4 Risk Bound and Rates ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.7</span></a> that elucidates the asymptotic dependence on <math id="S2.SS4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem7" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_proposition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem7.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition 2.7</span></span></h6>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.Thmtheorem7.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Under the same setting as Theorem <a href="#S2.Thmtheorem5" title="Theorem 2.5 (Risk Bound) ‣ 2.4 Risk Bound and Rates ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.5</span></a>, with probability at least <math id="S2.Thmtheorem7.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-\delta</annotation></semantics></math> for all <math id="S2.Thmtheorem7.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T\geq 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T\geq 1</annotation></semantics></math>, the excess SPO risk satisfies <math id="S2.Thmtheorem7.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="R_{\textnormal{SPO}}(h_{T})-R_{\textnormal{SPO}}^{*}\leq\mathcal{\tilde{O}}(T^{-1/2}\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>SPO</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>R</mi><mtext>SPO</mtext><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>≤</mo><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><msqrt><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\textnormal{SPO}}(h_{T})-R_{\textnormal{SPO}}^{*}\leq\mathcal{\tilde{O}}(T^{-1/2}\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)})</annotation></semantics></math>. Equivalently, with probability at least <math id="S2.Thmtheorem7.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-\delta</annotation></semantics></math>, there exists a stopping time <math id="S2.Thmtheorem7.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\sim\mathcal{\tilde{O}}(\epsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ϵ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\sim\mathcal{\tilde{O}}(\epsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta))</annotation></semantics></math> such that <math id="S2.Thmtheorem7.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\forall T\geq\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\forall T\geq\tau</annotation></semantics></math> we have <math id="S2.Thmtheorem7.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\textnormal{SPO}}(h_{T})-R_{\textnormal{SPO}}(h^{*})\leq\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>SPO</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>SPO</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\textnormal{SPO}}(h_{T})-R_{\textnormal{SPO}}(h^{*})\leq\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Proposition <a href="#S2.Thmtheorem7" title="Proposition 2.7 ‣ 2.4 Risk Bound and Rates ‣ 2 Algorithm and Performance Guarantees ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.7</span></a> implies a sample complexity on the order of <math id="S2.SS4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{\tilde{O}}(\epsilon^{-2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>ϵ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{\tilde{O}}(\epsilon^{-2})</annotation></semantics></math>, which matches the typical sample complexity of the supervised learning approach in the predict-then-optimize regime (e.g., <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">El Balghiti et al. (2022)</a></cite>). This result shows that the experimental design algorithm based on directional-uncertainty enjoys at least the same theoretical guarantees as these decision-blind approaches (e.g., see Theorem 2 for general reweighted regression problem in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Beygelzimer et al. (2009)</a></cite>). In the next section, we further compare our directional-uncertainty–based algorithm with the traditional <math id="S2.SS4.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-norm–based method.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Comparison with Decision-blind Sequential Design</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Traditional experimental design methods are typically decision-blind, focusing solely on improving predictive accuracy. However, for downstream linear optimization, the directional accuracy of parameter estimates is often more critical for decision quality than their overall magnitude (e.g., as measured by the <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> norm). In this section, we theoretically illustrate the advantages of our proposed design method by contrasting our directional-uncertainty approach with standard benchmarks, as summarized in Figure <a href="#S3.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 3 Comparison with Decision-blind Sequential Design ‣ Decision-Focused Sequential Experimental Design: A Directional Uncertainty-Guided Approach" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>.</p>
</div>
